name: Writing for the audience
sub: When the goal says who is reading
rule: Some goals name the reader: "an audience unfamiliar with" the topic, or one that already knows it. A new reader needs to be told what the thing is. A reader who already knows it does not.
trick: Find the audience words in the goal. If the reader is unfamiliar, the right sentence names the thing and says what it is in a few words. If the reader already knows it, skip the explaining.
passage:
Notes: A seed library lends seeds instead of books. Members plant the seeds at home. At the end of the season, they return seeds from their best plants. The Eastfield seed library opened in 2019.

Goal: Introduce the Eastfield seed library to an audience unfamiliar with seed libraries.

examples.text: The Eastfield seed library, which lends seeds instead of books, opened in 2019.
examples.note: Names it and says what a seed library is.

examples.text: Members of the Eastfield seed library return seeds from their best plants.
examples.note: True, but a new reader still has no idea what a seed library is.

another.text: Telling a friend about a game they have never played, you first say what kind of game it is. Telling a friend who plays it every day, you jump straight to the news. Same game, different listener, different first sentence.
another.example:
Never played: "It's a board game where you build towns."
Plays every day: "I finally won with three towns."

steps.say: Every choice uses true notes. The goal decides which one is right, and this goal names a reader.

options: Someone who has never heard of seed libraries
Someone who already uses the seed library
steps.hint: Look for the audience words at the end of the goal.

steps.ask: So what must the sentence do besides name the library?
options: Say what a seed library is
Give the year members return seeds
steps.then: A new reader needs the idea explained before anything else makes sense.
steps.line: Must explain: lends seeds instead of books

options: The Eastfield seed library, which lends seeds instead of books, opened in 2019.
Members of the Eastfield seed library return seeds from their best plants.
steps.then: The other one is true, but it skips what a seed library is.
steps.hint: Which one tells you what a seed library does?

questions.passage:
Notes: A tool library lends tools such as drills and ladders. Members borrow a tool for up to a week. The Riverside tool library has over 600 tools. It is run by volunteers.

Goal: Introduce the Riverside tool library to an audience unfamiliar with tool libraries.
questions.stem: Which sentence best meets the goal?
options: The Riverside tool library is run by volunteers and has over 600 tools.
The Riverside tool library lends drills, ladders and other tools, which members can borrow for up to a week.
Members of the Riverside tool library can keep a tool for up to a week.
questions.why: Only this one tells a new reader what a tool library actually does: it lends tools.

questions.passage:
Notes: The bike lane on Elm Street opened last spring. Riders had asked for it for years. Use doubled in its first month. Readers of the town cycling club newsletter already know the lane well.

Goal: Share a new fact about the Elm Street lane with readers of the cycling club newsletter.
questions.stem: Which sentence best meets the goal?
options: Use of the Elm Street bike lane doubled in its first month.
A bike lane is a part of the road set aside for people riding bikes.
Elm Street is a street in town where people ride bikes.
questions.why: These readers already know the lane, so explaining what a bike lane is wastes their time. The new fact is the doubling.

name: Putting results in order
sub: Listing results from lowest to highest
rule: To put results in order, find each value in the table first, then sort them. Read the question again to see which way: increasing means smallest first, decreasing means largest first.
trick: Write each value next to its name before you look at the choices. Then check only the first and last item of each choice; that rules most of them out fast.

examples.note: Flip it: Rubber, Golf, Tennis, Foam.

another.text: Lining kids up for a class photo by height, you don't guess. You look at each kid, then put the shortest at one end and the tallest at the other. If the teacher says tallest first, you just start from the other end.
another.example:
Heights: Sam 120, Ana 135, Leo 128
Shortest first: Sam, Leo, Ana

steps.say: First find every value. Then sort. Then check which way the question wants it.

steps.hint: Find the smallest number in the bounce column.

steps.ask: The question asks for increasing bounce height. Which end comes first?

steps.then: 15, 48, 55, 62. Rubber, Golf, Tennis, Foam has the right balls, but from greatest to least.

questions.stem: Which list puts the balls in order of decreasing bounce height?
Which list puts the liquids in order of increasing time to boil?
questions.why: Increasing means shortest time first: 5, 6, 8 minutes.

name: What each scientist thinks
rule: When a passage gives two or more scientists' explanations, sum up each one's main claim in one short sentence before you answer. A question about what one scientist would say, or what they all agree on, is answered from those sentences.
trick: For an "agree" question, the right choice is something every viewpoint says or takes for granted, often a fact stated before they start to disagree. If even one scientist would reject it, cross it off.
passage:
Scientist 1: Birds fly south in fall because the days get shorter. Shorter days trigger the urge to migrate.

Scientist 2: Birds fly south in fall because their food runs out. When insects disappear in the cold, birds leave to find more.

examples.note: Birds fly south in fall. They only disagree about why.

another.text: Two friends argue about why the cookies are gone. One says the dog ate them. The other says little brother did. They disagree about who, but they both agree on one thing: the cookies are gone.
another.example:
Friend 1: the dog. Friend 2: little brother.
Both agree: the cookies are gone.

steps.say: Before any question, give each scientist one short sentence.

options: Shorter days cause birds to migrate
Running out of food causes birds to migrate
Running out of food causes birds to migrate

steps.ask: Which statement would both scientists agree with?
options: Birds fly south in the fall.
Shorter days are the main cause of migration.
Birds leave only when insects disappear.
steps.then: They argue about why, not whether, birds fly south.
steps.hint: Scientist 2 would reject the claim about shorter days, and Scientist 1 the claim about insects.
steps.line: ✓ Both: birds fly south in fall

questions.passage:
Student 1: Ice floats because it is less dense than liquid water.

Student 2: Ice floats because tiny air bubbles are trapped inside it.
questions.stem: Both students would most likely agree that:
options: air bubbles are the reason ice floats.
ice is less dense than liquid water.
questions.why: They disagree about the reason, but both explain why ice floats, so both accept that it does.

questions.passage:
Scientist 1: The lake's fish died because the water got too warm.

Scientist 2: The lake's fish died because a factory leaked chemicals into the water.
questions.stem: According to Scientist 2, what would most likely have prevented the fish from dying?
options: Adding more fish to the lake
questions.why: Scientist 2 blames the chemicals, so stopping the leak would remove the cause.

name: Testing a "double" claim
rule: A claim that one thing is directly proportional to another means doubling the first doubles the second. To test it, find two rows where the first value doubles and see whether the second value doubles too.
trick: Going up is not enough. If the first value doubles and the second only goes up a little, the claim is wrong.

examples.note: Mass doubled and stretch doubled: proportional.
Stretch went up, but it did not double: not proportional.

another.text: One cookie costs 2 dollars and two cookies cost 4 dollars. Twice the cookies, twice the price: that's proportional. But if two cookies cost 3 dollars, the price went up without doubling, so it isn't.
another.example:
1 cookie $2, 2 cookies $4 → proportional
1 cookie $2, 2 cookies $3 → not proportional

steps.say: Claim: the stretch is directly proportional to the mass. Test it with two rows where the mass doubles.

steps.ask: Which two rows show the mass doubling?
Between those rows, what happens to the stretch?
options: 3 → 6 cm, it goes up by 3, so it does not double
steps.then: Twice 3 is 6, so going up by 3 here is exactly doubling.

steps.ask: Check one more pair: 100 g to 200 g. Does the stretch double?
options: No, it only goes up by 6

steps.then: Every time the mass doubles, the stretch doubles.

questions.stem: A student claims plant height is directly proportional to hours of light. Is the claim supported?
options: Yes, because height increases as light increases
No, because doubling the light from 6 to 12 hours did not double the height
questions.why: Light doubled from 6 to 12 hours, but height went from 10 to 14 cm, not to 20. Going up is not the same as doubling.

questions.stem: Based on the table, if the volume is doubled, the mass will:
questions.why: 20 → 40 mL gives 20 → 40 g, and 40 → 80 mL gives 40 → 80 g. Each time the volume doubles, so does the mass.
